title: Quiet, not lazy
objective: Recognize delirium as an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness and cognition, in hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed forms; the quiet hypoactive form is the one most often missed
secondaryObjectives: Treat polypharmacy (regular use of 5 or more medicines) as a risk factor in older adults, linked to falls, frailty, disability and death
Pharmacology in older adults: polypharmacy, fall-risk medications and exercise interactions

brief.situation: 09:30 on an orthopedic ward. You are the acute care physical therapist. Mrs. Okafor, 84, is on day 3 after hip fracture repair. The nurse's note says she was 'unmotivated' and declined physical therapy yesterday. Her daughter says she was 'sharp as a tack' and doing her own crossword last week.
handover: The surgeon's order: weight bearing as tolerated, walk twice a day.
Hospital policy: report any acute change in mental status to the nurse and the medical team straight away.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: An unrecognized delirium deepens and her fall risk climbs. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

why.question: Why is Mrs. Okafor quiet and 'unmotivated', and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Possible hypoactive delirium: she cannot sustain attention, the change began after surgery and fluctuates, and she was sharp last week; eleven medicines plus overnight sedating medicine and an opioid are likely contributors.
parts.modelAnswer: She's probably got hypoactive delirium. She can't keep her attention, it started after surgery and comes and goes, and she was sharp last week. Her pile of meds and the overnight sedative may be part of it.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Report the acute change to the nurse and medical team now with the medication concern; adapt the session to bed-level and sitting work with orientation aids; no forced walking; document.
parts.modelAnswer: Tell the nurse and team now and flag the meds, keep today to bed and sitting work with her glasses and hearing aid on, don't force walking, and write it up.

fall.headline: Fall on a new hip
fall.body: A quiet, sleepy older adult after surgery may have hypoactive delirium, the form most often missed. Test attention, compare with baseline, report it, and adapt the session.

safe.headline: Delirium recognized
safe.body: You tested attention, found an acute fluctuating change from her baseline, adapted the session and told the team within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness and cognition; the quiet hypoactive form is the one most often missed and is easily mislabeled as low motivation. Mrs. Okafor fails a simple attention task, was sharp last week and fluctuates through the day. Polypharmacy (5 or more regular medicines) is a risk factor linked to falls, and she is on eleven plus sedating medicine. Report the acute change to the team, adapt the session and do not force walking.

formQ.ask: While you assess: which form of delirium is most often missed?
formQ.explain: The quiet hypoactive form is the one most often missed.
